title: Spherical Mirrors: Reflection, Sign Convention, and Image Formation
short_intro: Spherical mirrors are reflecting surfaces that form a part of a hollow sphere of glass or metal. They obey the laws of reflection and are categorized into concave and convex mirrors based on the curvature of their reflecting surfaces.

exam_scope.tgt_core: Reflection laws, mirror formula, relation between focal length and radius of curvature, real and virtual image characteristics, linear magnification, and standard ray diagrams for concave and convex mirrors.
exam_scope.pgt_extension: Longitudinal and areal magnification, velocity of image in moving mirror problems, aberration in spherical mirrors (spherical aberration), and optical bench methods for focal length determination.

prerequisites: Geometry of circles and spheres (radius, pole, tangent)
Real and virtual images in geometrical optics

concept_notes.heading: Sign Convention (New Cartesian Sign Convention)
bullets: All distances are measured from the pole (P) of the spherical mirror as the origin.
Distances measured in the direction of incident light are taken as positive, while those measured opposite to the direction of incident light are taken as negative.
Heights measured perpendicularly upwards from the principal axis are positive, and those measured downwards are negative.

concept_notes.heading: Focus and Focal Length
bullets: Paraxial rays parallel to the principal axis converge to (concave) or appear to diverge from (convex) a fixed point on the principal axis called the principal focus (F).
The distance between the pole and the principal focus is the focal length (f).
For paraxial rays, the focal length is related to the radius of curvature (R) by the relation f = R / 2.

concept_notes.heading: Nature of Images Formed
bullets: A concave mirror can form real, inverted images as well as virtual, erect images depending on the object position.
A convex mirror always forms a virtual, erect, and diminished image for any real position of the object.
Linear magnification (m) is positive for virtual images and negative for real images.

concept_notes.heading: Spherical Aberration
bullets: Marginal rays falling at large heights from the principal axis do not converge at the principal focus F, a phenomenon known as spherical aberration.
This defect leads to a blurred image, which can be minimized by using parabolic mirrors or stop diaphragms to block marginal rays.
Paraxial rays alone strictly satisfy the mirror formula.

derivations.title: Mirror Formula for a Concave Mirror (Real Image)
derivations.conditions: Paraxial rays, object placed beyond the focus of a concave mirror forming a real image.
steps: Consider a concave mirror with pole P, focus F, and center of curvature C. Let an object AB be placed beyond C.
Using similar triangles ABC and A'B'C, the ratio of heights gives AB / A'B' = BC / B'C.
Similarly, using triangles ABP and A'B'P, AB / A'B' = PB / PB'.
Equating the two ratios and substituting Cartesian coordinates (PB = -u, PB' = -v, PC = -R = -2f), we get (-u - (-2f)) / (-2f - (-v)) = -u / -v.
Simplifying the algebraic relation yields (1 / v) + (1 / u) = (1 / f).

derivations.title: Relation between Focal Length and Radius of Curvature
derivations.conditions: Paraxial rays incident on a concave mirror at small angles.
steps: Let a ray parallel to the principal axis strike the concave mirror at point M at a height h from the pole P.
Let C be the center of curvature and angle MCP = theta. Since the ray is parallel, angle PMF = theta and angle MCF = 2theta.
In triangle MCP, tan(theta) = h / PC approx theta. In triangle MKF (where MK is perpendicular to principal axis), tan(2theta) = h / PF approx 2theta.
Substituting theta and 2theta gives h / PF = 2 (h / PC), which simplifies to PC = 2 PF.
Since PC = R and PF = f, we obtain R = 2f.

graphs_and_experiments.title: u-v Graph for a Concave Mirror
graphs_and_experiments.what_to_draw: A rectangular hyperbola plotted in the second quadrant where both u and v are negative, with asymptotes at u = f and v = f.
graphs_and_experiments.interpretation: Shows the inverse non-linear relationship between object distance and image distance. The intersection with the line v = u gives the center of curvature (u = -2f, v = -2f).
graphs_and_experiments.exam_use: Tested conceptually to identify focal length from intercept values or symmetry lines.

graphs_and_experiments.title: Magnification (m) vs Object Distance (u)
graphs_and_experiments.what_to_draw: A curve showing m starting from 0 at u = infinity, going to -infinity as u approaches f from the left, and positive values for virtual images when u < f.
graphs_and_experiments.interpretation: Represents the transition from real inverted (negative m) to virtual erect (positive m) images.
graphs_and_experiments.exam_use: Used in numerical problems involving threshold object positions where magnification magnitude equals 1.

graphs_and_experiments.title: Optical Bench Experiment for Focal Length
graphs_and_experiments.what_to_draw: Experimental setup schematic showing an illuminated pin, a concave mirror on a stand, and a screen mounted on an optical bench.
graphs_and_experiments.interpretation: Determines focal length by locating the coincidence position where the object pin and its real inverted image coincide at the center of curvature (u = v = R = 2f).
graphs_and_experiments.exam_use: Core practical physics question in viva and conceptual MCQ formats.

solved_numericals.question: An object of height 2 cm is placed at a distance of 30 cm in front of a concave mirror of focal length 20 cm. Find the position, nature, and height of the image.
solution_steps: Identify given values using sign convention: u = -30 cm, f = -20 cm, ho = +2 cm.
Calculate height using magnification: hi = - (v/u) * ho = - (-60 / -30) * 2 = -2 * 2 = -4 cm.
solved_numericals.answer: Image distance v = -60 cm (real and in front of mirror), height = -4 cm (inverted and enlarged).

solved_numericals.question: A small rod of length 10 cm is placed along the principal axis of a concave mirror of focal length 30 cm, such that its nearer end is at a distance of 40 cm from the mirror. Find the length of the image of the rod.
solution_steps: Focal length f = -30 cm. Distance of nearer end u1 = -40 cm. Distance of farther end u2 = -(40 + 10) = -50 cm.
Length of the image is the distance between the two image positions: delta v = |v1 - v2| = |-120 - (-75)| = 45 cm.

solved_numericals.question: A concave mirror has a focal length of 20 cm. At what distance from the mirror should an object be placed so that the size of the image is twice the size of the object, and the image is real?
solution_steps: For a real image formed by a concave mirror, magnification m = -2.
Use the magnification formula relating m, f, and u: m = f / (f - u).
solved_numericals.answer: 30 cm in front of the mirror (u = -30 cm)

assumptions_and_limitations: Mirrors are assumed to have a small aperture so that paraxial ray approximations (sin(theta) approx theta) hold true.
The mirror formula fails for wide-aperture spherical mirrors due to spherical aberration.
Wavelength of light is assumed to be much smaller than the mirror dimensions, so diffraction effects can be neglected.

common_misconceptions.wrong: A convex mirror can produce a real image if the object is placed beyond its focus.
common_misconceptions.correct: A convex mirror always produces a virtual, erect, and diminished image for any real object.
common_misconceptions.why: The reflecting surface bulges outward, causing parallel or convergent incident rays to always diverge after reflection.

common_misconceptions.wrong: The focal length of a concave mirror changes when it is immersed in water.
common_misconceptions.correct: The focal length of a spherical mirror remains unchanged in water.
common_misconceptions.why: Reflection depends only on the law of reflection (angles of incidence and reflection), which is independent of the surrounding medium's refractive index.

common_misconceptions.wrong: Power of a mirror has units of dioptres only when focal length is in centimeters.
common_misconceptions.correct: Power is measured in dioptres when the focal length is expressed strictly in meters (P = -1/f).
common_misconceptions.why: Dimensional consistency requires focal length to be in meters for the dioptre (m^-1) unit.

quick_revision: For a concave mirror, f is negative; for a convex mirror, f is positive.
Real images are always inverted and formed on the same side as the object; virtual images are erect and formed behind the mirror.
Longitudinal magnification is equal to the negative square of transverse magnification (-m^2).
